title: Repository Pattern
readme:
FULL STACK DEVELOPER 2026
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture
Phase 24 - Repository Pattern

This phase introduces a focused TaskRepository only after persistence complexity justifies it. It rejects generic CRUD wrappers and preserves transaction correctness over architectural purity.

lessons.body:
When a Repository Earns Its Place
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24

The smell is not Prisma itself
Prisma is already a strong type-safe data access API. Wrapping every single Prisma call with an
identical method such as repository.findMany() usually adds no architectural value. The useful
pressure appears when business services need to stop knowing detailed relation filters,
pagination/count mechanics, persistence mapping, or testing setup.

Before the repository
TasksService
-> Prisma task.findMany(...deep authorization scope...)
-> Prisma task.count(...same where...)
-> Prisma error codes
-> relation include/select shapes
-> business rules
-> workflow decisions

After a useful repository
TasksService
-> taskRepository.listScoped(userId, query)
-> business rules
-> workflow decisions

PrismaTaskRepository
-> Prisma where/orderBy/select
-> count + page query
-> persistence mapping

Decision checklist
• Would the service become easier to read if query construction moved out?

• Do multiple workflows need the same complex persistence query?

• Do unit tests currently need extensive Prisma-shaped mocks?

• Would a stable application-owned result type reduce persistence leakage?

• Can you name repository operations in business/persistence language more meaningful than
generic CRUD?

lessons.title: Design the TaskRepository Contract
lessons.summary: Design the TaskRepository Contract Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24 Design from the consumer inward Start from what TasksService actually needs. lessons.body:
Design the TaskRepository Contract
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24

Design from the consumer inward
Start from what TasksService actually needs. Do not start by reproducing every Prisma method.
A repository contract is an application boundary, not an ORM compatibility layer.

Feature-owned contract
export interface TaskRepository {
findById(id: string): Promise<TaskRecord | null>

findScopedById(
taskId: string,
userId: string,
): Promise<TaskRecord | null>

listScoped(
userId: string,
query: TaskListQuery,
): Promise<PaginatedTasks>

create(input: CreateTaskRecord): Promise<TaskRecord>
update(id: string, input: UpdateTaskRecord): Promise<TaskRecord>
delete(id: string): Promise<void>
}

Contract design rules
• Return application-owned shapes when persistence independence is worth the mapping cost.

• Keep HTTP request/response concerns out of the repository.

• Do not put authorization decisions in the repository; it may enforce a caller-provided scope,
while the service decides the policy.

• Prefer methods that capture meaningful query intent over dozens of tiny ORM wrappers.

• Keep the interface inside the feature until more features genuinely need a shared abstraction.

lessons.summary: PrismaTaskRepository: Query and Mapping Implementation Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24 Persistence details belong here The implementation owns Prisma relation filters, ordering, select/include decisions, error-code translation that is truly persistence-specific, and mapping from generated records into stable repository result shapes. Scoped list…
lessons.body:
PrismaTaskRepository: Query and
Mapping Implementation
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24

Persistence details belong here
The implementation owns Prisma relation filters, ordering, select/include decisions, error-code
translation that is truly persistence-specific, and mapping from generated records into stable
repository result shapes.

Scoped list example
async listScoped(
userId: string,
query: TaskListQuery,
): Promise<PaginatedTasks> {
const where = this.buildScopedWhere(userId, query)
const orderBy = this.buildOrderBy(query)
const skip = (query.page - 1) * query.pageSize

const [rows, totalItems] = await this.prisma.$transaction([
this.prisma.task.findMany({
where,
orderBy,
skip,
take: query.pageSize,
select: taskListSelect,
}),
this.prisma.task.count({ where }),
])

return mapPage(rows, totalItems, query)
}

Why this is useful
• The service no longer knows Prisma relation syntax.

• The count and data query cannot accidentally build different filters.

• Sorting allow-lists stay close to persistence mapping.

• Changing select/include structure does not force business-service edits.

Do not hide everything
A repository should hide persistence mechanics that the service should not care about. It should
not hide important business decisions by burying them in database code.

lessons.summary: Refactor TasksService to Business Intent Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24 Before A service method that mixes policy, Prisma query construction, mapping, and database error handling becomes difficult to scan. After async getTaskForUser( taskId: string, currentUser: CurrentUser, ) { const task =…
lessons.body:
Refactor TasksService to Business
Intent
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24

Before
A service method that mixes policy, Prisma query construction, mapping, and database error
handling becomes difficult to scan.

After
async getTaskForUser(
taskId: string,
currentUser: CurrentUser,
) {
const task = await this.tasks.findScopedById(
taskId,
currentUser.id,
)

if (!task) {
throw new TaskNotFoundException(taskId)
}

return task
}

Responsibility split
Controller                     HTTP method, params/body/query, status codes, decorators.

Service                        Business policy, workflow, invariants, authorization decisions.

Repository                     Persistence queries, scopes supplied by the service, mapping, database-facing
mechanics.

PrismaService                  Generated Prisma Client lifecycle and connection/adapter concerns.

The service still owns meaning
A repository may return null. The service decides whether that means Task-not-found, hidden
cross-tenant resource, optional relationship, or some other domain outcome.

lessons.title: Transactions and the Repository Boundary
lessons.summary: Transactions and the Repository Boundary Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24 Repositories make transactions harder if designed carelessly A transaction spanning Task, Membership, Project, audit records, and notifications is an application workflow. Hiding every table behind an isolated repository can make it…
lessons.body:
Transactions and the Repository
Boundary
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24

Repositories make transactions harder if designed
carelessly
A transaction spanning Task, Membership, Project, audit records, and notifications is an
application workflow. Hiding every table behind an isolated repository can make it difficult to
guarantee that all writes share the same Prisma transaction client.

TaskFlow decision
Phase 24 does not introduce a generic UnitOfWork or transaction manager yet. Single-repository
atomic operations may use Prisma transactions internally. Cross-feature transactional
orchestration remains explicit until repeated pressure justifies a dedicated abstraction.

Good internal transaction
const [rows, total] = await prisma.$transaction([
prisma.task.findMany({ where, ...page }),
prisma.task.count({ where }),
])

Warning sign
service -> TaskRepository
-> MembershipRepository
-> AuditRepository
-> ??? how do all three share one transaction?

Rule
Do not weaken atomicity just to preserve a repository pattern. Persistence
abstraction is secondary to correctness.

Prisma context
Prisma 7 still distinguishes nested writes, sequential/batch transactions, and interactive
transactions. Those mechanics remain implementation concerns, but the transaction boundary
should be chosen by the application workflow.

lessons.title: Query Specific Repositories vs Generic CRUD
lessons.summary: Query-Specific Repositories vs Generic CRUD Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24 The generic repository trap Generic repository trap GenericRepository<T> TaskRepository find / create / update / delete listScoped / findContext / create Mirrors ORM and hides useful query semantics Names persistence operations…
lessons.body:
Query-Specific Repositories vs Generic
CRUD
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24

The generic repository trap
Generic repository trap

GenericRepository<T>                                                     TaskRepository

find / create / update / delete                                  listScoped / findContext / create

Mirrors ORM and hides useful query semantics                  Names persistence operations the service actually needs

Figure 24.1 - The generic repository trap

Generic wrapper example
interface Repository<T> {
findAll(): Promise<T[]>
findById(id: string): Promise<T | null>
create(data: Partial<T>): Promise<T>
update(id: string, data: Partial<T>): Promise<T>
delete(id: string): Promise<void>
}

Why it often fails
This contract is so broad that complex filtering, scoped authorization, relations, partial updates,
transactions, bulk operations, and database-specific capabilities soon leak through anyway. It
often recreates a weaker ORM on top of a stronger ORM.

Prefer feature semantics
• listScoped(userId, query)

• findForAssignment(taskId)

• findByIdInWorkspace(taskId, workspaceId)

• createFromProject(projectId, data)

Not every query needs a repository method
If a one-off reporting query appears later, evaluate it independently. A read-model/query service
may be clearer than bloating TaskRepository with unrelated analytics.

lessons.body:
Repository Integration Tests with
PostgreSQL
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24

Test the real adapter separately
The concrete Prisma repository should be tested against a real disposable/resettable PostgreSQL
database because its job is to translate the contract into real persistence behavior. Current
Prisma guidance explicitly distinguishes unit tests with mocks from integration tests against a
real test database.

Integration scope
• Apply migrations to a test database.

• Seed the minimum Workspace/User/Membership/Project graph.

• Call PrismaTaskRepository directly.

• Verify scoped reads cannot cross Workspaces.

• Verify pagination count and rows share filters.

• Verify sorting and nullable relations.

• Reset data between tests.

Two boundaries
Two different questions require two different test boundaries

Service unit test                                   Repository integration test
TasksService -> FakeTaskRepository                        PrismaTaskRepository -> PostgreSQL
No PostgreSQL required                                     Real migrations + queries

Proves business decisions                                   Proves SQL/query mapping

Figure 24.1 - Two boundaries

Why both matter
A service unit test can pass while a Prisma where clause is wrong. A repository integration test
can pass while business policy is wrong. Keep the questions separate.

lessons.body:
Mapping, Persistence Types and
Leakage Trade-offs
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24

Three choices
A repository can return Prisma-generated types, application-owned structural records, or full
domain entities. Each option has a different cost. TaskFlow chooses application-owned structural
records without introducing rich domain entity classes yet.

Trade-off table
Option                        Benefit                   Cost

Prisma types                  Least mapping             Strong persistence coupling

App records                   Stable service contract   Some mapping code

Domain entities               Rich behavior boundary    Highest complexity; not earned yet

Example application-owned record
export type TaskRecord = {
id: string
projectId: string
assigneeId: string | null
title: string
description: string | null
status: TaskStatus
priority: TaskPriority
dueAt: Date | null
completedAt: Date | null
createdAt: Date
updatedAt: Date
}

Rule
Mapping is justified when it buys a stable boundary. Do not create mapper classes for every
object merely to satisfy a diagram.

lessons.title: Incremental Adoption and Anti Patterns
lessons.summary: Incremental Adoption and Anti-Patterns Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24 Do not big-bang refactor TaskFlow migrates read/list and straightforward write paths first. Transaction-heavy or cross-feature persistence can remain direct Prisma temporarily if forcing it behind the new boundary would make correctness harder…
lessons.body:
Incremental Adoption and
Anti-Patterns
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24

Do not big-bang refactor
TaskFlow migrates read/list and straightforward write paths first. Transaction-heavy or
cross-feature persistence can remain direct Prisma temporarily if forcing it behind the new
boundary would make correctness harder to see.

Migration path
Step 1   identify repeated/complex persistence logic
Step 2   define the smallest useful contract
Step 3   implement Prisma adapter
Step 4   bind with Nest DI token
Step 5   move one service path at a time
Step 6   add fake service tests
Step 7   add repository integration tests
Step 8   reassess remaining direct Prisma usage

Anti-patterns
• One repository interface per Prisma model by default.

• A generic repository that only renames Prisma methods.

• Repositories throwing HTTP exceptions.

• Repositories deciding user permissions instead of receiving an already-decided scope.

• Mapping every field through ceremonial classes with no boundary benefit.

• Breaking transaction atomicity to keep repositories pure.

• Assuming repository means the application is database-agnostic in practice.

Success criterion
The repository is successful when TasksService becomes easier to read and test while
persistence correctness remains explicit. File count is not the metric.

lessons.body:
Hands-On Lab and Phase Exit
Volume 07 - Advanced Application Architecture | Phase 24

Lab 1 - Identify pressure
Open the current TasksService. Mark each line as HTTP concern, business policy, authorization
policy, persistence query, persistence mapping, or transaction concern. Only the persistence
categories are candidates for TaskRepository.

Lab 2 - Extract listScoped
• Define TaskRepository.listScoped().

• Move Prisma where, sorting, skip/take, and count logic into PrismaTaskRepository.

• Keep filter semantics and authorization policy clear.

• Verify the API response does not change.

Lab 3 - Replace the provider in a unit test
• Create FakeTaskRepository.

• Use TASK_REPOSITORY with useValue.

• Test one valid status transition.

• Test one invalid transition.

• Confirm no database is required.

Lab 4 - Integration verification
• Use a dedicated test PostgreSQL database.

• Apply migrations.

• Create two Workspaces and memberships.

• Verify a scoped repository query never returns the other Workspace Task.

• Verify pagination metadata matches the filtered rows.

Engineer challenge
Design how you would support a cross-repository transaction involving Task assignment,
Membership validation, and an AuditLog write. Compare: direct Prisma orchestration, a
UnitOfWork/transaction context, or a purpose-built persistence operation. Do not implement the
most abstract option automatically; justify the cost.

Phase exit checklist
• I can explain why Prisma does not automatically require a repository wrapper.

• I can design a contract from service needs rather than ORM methods.

• I can bind an interface-shaped dependency with a NestJS Symbol token.

• I can test business logic with a fake repository.

• I know why repository integration tests still need PostgreSQL.

• I can identify the generic-repository trap.

• I can protect transaction correctness even when the abstraction is imperfect.

Sources used in this phase
Source                                              Use in this phase

NestJS - Custom providers                           Interfaces are erased at runtime; custom string/symbol
https://docs.nestjs.com/fundamentals/custom-pr      tokens can bind an interface contract to a concrete provider.
oviders

NestJS - Testing                                    TestingModule can replace/override providers so business
https://docs.nestjs.com/fundamentals/testing        services can be tested against doubles.

Prisma ORM v7 - Unit testing                        Prisma documents dependency injection and mocking as
https://docs.prisma.io/docs/orm/prisma-client/tes   valid unit-testing approaches.
ting/unit-testing

Prisma ORM v7 - Best practices                      Current Prisma guidance separates unit tests with mocks
https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7/more/best-pr      from integration tests against a resettable database.
actices

Prisma ORM v7 - Transactions                        Nested writes, batch transactions, and interactive
https://docs.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7/prisma-client/   transactions remain persistence-specific concerns.
queries/transactions

Purpose

lessons.body:
Guided Build Lab — Phase 24: Repository Pattern

Purpose
Introduce repository boundaries only where they improve persistence isolation, domain language, testing, or future changeability.

Deliverable
One TaskFlow aggregate/use case refactored behind a purposeful repository interface with real database integration tests.

Before you touch the code
Open the previous phase checkpoint, run the repository's verification commands, and make sure Git is clean. A guided lab is useful only when you know which change introduced a failure. Write down the current browser/API/database behavior you expect before modifying anything.

Architecture trace
service/use case -> repository interface -> Prisma implementation -> database -> mapped domain/application result

Read this flow left to right, then right to left. For each arrow, say what data crosses the boundary, which side trusts the other, and what evidence would prove that this boundary works. This habit prevents framework APIs from becoming disconnected memorization.

Step 1 — Choose a service whose persistence queries are complex enough to justify a boundary.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 2 — Write repository methods in application language rather than generic findAll/create/update/delete.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 3 — Move Prisma-specific selection/query details into the implementation.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 4 — Decide whether persistence types may cross the boundary or need mapping and document the trade-off.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 5 — Unit-test service behavior with a fake only where it proves useful behavior.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 6 — Integration-test the real repository against PostgreSQL so fake and implementation do not drift.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Checkpoint
When the lab works, inspect git diff. Remove accidental debugging output and unrelated edits. Run type checking/tests/build commands relevant to this phase. Commit the checkpoint with a message that describes the capability added, not merely the files changed.

Explain-back
Without looking at the lesson, explain why each layer in the architecture trace exists, what this phase added to TaskFlow, and what would break if the new responsibility were moved to the wrong layer. If you cannot explain the boundary, repeat the trace before moving on.

lessons.title: Debugging Workshop
lessons.summary:
Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.
lessons.body:
Debugging Workshop — Phase 24: Repository Pattern

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
service/use case -> repository interface -> Prisma implementation -> database -> mapped domain/application result

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — GenericRepository<T> mirroring ORM methods
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Repository wrapping every trivial Prisma call with no value
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — Mocks proving an imaginary database behavior
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 4 — Mapping everything into duplicate types without a domain need
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Repository Pattern

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 24 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Introduce repository boundaries only where they improve persistence isolation, domain language, testing, or future changeability.

Required artifact
One TaskFlow aggregate/use case refactored behind a purposeful repository interface with real database integration tests.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can explain when not to use a repository.
• Can design task-specific repository methods.
• Can test both service and real persistence.
• Can identify ORM leakage tradeoffs.

Independent build sequence
1. Choose a service whose persistence queries are complex enough to justify a boundary.
2. Write repository methods in application language rather than generic findAll/create/update/delete.
3. Move Prisma-specific selection/query details into the implementation.
4. Decide whether persistence types may cross the boundary or need mapping and document the trade-off.
5. Unit-test service behavior with a fake only where it proves useful behavior.
6. Integration-test the real repository against PostgreSQL so fake and implementation do not drift.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

lessons.body:
Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 24: Repository Pattern. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
One TaskFlow aggregate/use case refactored behind a purposeful repository interface with real database integration tests.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

references.preview:
# ADR - Introduce TaskRepository incrementally

## Decision
Introduce TaskRepository for complex/scoped Task persistence queries and straightforward writes. Do not create GenericRepository<T>. Do not force all cross-feature transactions behind repositories yet.

## Why now
TasksService now contains enough persistence-specific query construction that it obscures business intent and complicates unit testing.

## Consequences
- Service unit tests can use a fake repository.
- Prisma query behavior moves into integration-tested adapter code.
- Some direct Prisma orchestration may remain temporarily where transaction correctness would otherwise become less clear.

# TaskFlow Phase 24 - Repository Pattern

This snapshot introduces a focused TaskRepository boundary without converting the entire application into a generic repository architecture.

Default architecture:
- TasksService owns business policy and workflow meaning.
- TaskRepository defines persistence operations the service actually needs.
- PrismaTaskRepository implements those operations with Prisma 7.9.1.
- Cross-feature transaction abstraction is intentionally deferred until repeated pressure justifies it.

# Sources

- NestJS - Custom providers: https://docs.nestjs.com/fundamentals/custom-providers - Interfaces are erased at runtime; custom string/symbol tokens can bind an interface contract to a concrete provider.
- NestJS - Testing: https://docs.nestjs.com/fundamentals/testing - TestingModule can replace/override providers so business services can be tested against doubles.
- Prisma ORM v7 - Unit testing: https://docs.prisma.io/docs/orm/prisma-client/testing/unit-testing - Prisma documents dependency injection and mocking as valid unit-testing approaches.
- Prisma ORM v7 - Best practices: https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7/more/best-practices - Current Prisma guidance separates unit tests with mocks from integration tests against a resettable database.
- Prisma ORM v7 - Transactions: https://docs.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7/prisma-client/queries/transactions - Nested writes, batch transactions, and interactive transactions remain persistence-specific concerns.
